vt14_canon.topic: How the Christian biblical canon formed; Nicaea; Nag Hammadi; the Index

claims.text: Athanasius's 39th Festal Letter (367) lists the 27 NT books; calls apocryphal books 'an invention of heretics'; names Wisdom, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the Teaching (Didache) and the Shepherd as 'not indeed included in the Canon' but 'appointed by the Fathers to be read'; contains no order to destroy or burn books
Muratorian fragment usually dated late 2nd century (c.170-200), a minority prefers 4th century
Hippo 393 first council said to accept the present NT canon; its summary re-read and accepted at Carthage 397 and 419; Augustine regarded the canon as closed

The 382 Council of Rome list depends on the Decretum Gelasianum, probably a 6th-century compilation (Dobschütz); Hahneman, Gallagher and Rothschild argue it is not a decree of 382, since Jerome never mentions it; Jurgens holds the canon section authentic

East: Eastern churches less concerned to define sharply; Revelation accepted in the East by the 5th century with exceptions; Armenian Bible added Revelation c.1200; Syriac Peshitta originally lacked 2 Peter, 2-3 John, Jude, Revelation

Nicaea 325: at least 200 bishops, contemporary reports 250-300, traditional 318; signatory lists contain 200-220 names; all but two bishops subscribed; Arius, Theonas and Secundus refused, were excommunicated and exiled to Illyria; Arius's works ordered burned; decided the Arian question (creed, homoousios), Easter computation, Melitian schism, 20 canons; no record of any discussion of the biblical canon; the altar-falling-books story comes from the Synodicon Vetus (887)
Eusebius of Caesarea ascribes homoousios to Constantine; Constantine and Hosius supported the homoousian side

Trent Session IV, 8 April 1546, Decree concerning the Canonical Scriptures lists OT incl. Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Baruch, 1-2 Maccabees, and the 27 NT books; anathema on whoever does not accept them 'in their entirety and with all their parts'; Vulgate held 'as authentic'; vote 24-15 with 16 abstentions; identical list approved at Florence 4 February 1442

Luther's 1534 Bible placed the Apocrypha in a separate section 'Not Held Equal to the Scriptures, but Are Useful and Good to Read'; KJV 1611 included them; Protestant Bibles 66 books (39+27); Westminster Confession 1646: Apocrypha 'not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon'; BFBS 1825/26 excluded them from printing
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo narrower canon 81 books incl. 1 Enoch, Jubilees, 1-3 Meqabyan; broader canon adds church-order books

Nag Hammadi: found late 1945 by Muhammad Ali al-Samman; twelve codices plus a tractate from a thirteenth, 52 mostly Gnostic treatises in Coptic, 4th-century manuscripts; Coptic Museum Cairo; Robinson's burial-after-367 hypothesis is a proposal; Lewis & Blount 2014 propose private burial; facsimiles 1972-77, English 1977

Index: first Roman Index 1559 under Paul IV; Tridentine Index 1564; Congregation of the Index 1571, abolished 1917 and its work transferred to the Holy Office; last edition 1948 (about 4,000 titles); suppressed 14 June 1966 by CDF notification signed by Ottaviani, keeping 'moral value'; banned authors included Hume, Hobbes, Zola, Sartre, Descartes, Kant, Copernicus, Galileo

vt14_apostolic_archive.topic: The Vatican Apostolic Archive (formerly 'Secret'): name, size, access, holdings; the Library

claims.text: Motu proprio of 22 October 2019 (published 28 October 2019) renamed the Archivum Secretum the Vatican Apostolic Archive; 'Secret' meant 'the Pope's private, separate, reserved archive'; the word had acquired 'ambiguous, even negative nuances'; archive created at Paul V's behest c.1610-1612; name 'Secretum' attested from c.1646; opened to researchers of every country in 1881 under Leo XIII

About 85 linear km of shelving incl. an underground 'Bunker' under the Cortile della Pigna; over 600 fonds covering the 8th-20th centuries; access free and granted by pontificate, current limit end of Pius XII's pontificate (October 1958); scholars of all nationalities regardless of faith (as of 22 Aug 2025)

Wikipedia: reading room opened 1 January 1881; applicants qualified scholars from higher-education institutions with introductory letter; five items at a time; max sixty researchers a day; no pens or cameras; holdings include Henry VIII's annulment request, Galileo trial transcript, Michelangelo letters, 1521 bull excommunicating Luther; papal registers continuous from Innocent III
Pius XI (1922-39) files opened 18 September 2006 by decision of Benedict XVI, announced 29 June 2006 by Chappin and Pagano

Vatican Library: more than 80,000 manuscripts, more than 1.6 million printed volumes, some 8,600 incunabula; enlarged by Nicholas V and Sixtus IV; Library and Archive distinguished institutionally under Paul V; about 6,000 scholars use the Library
Francis, 4 March 2019: opening of Pius XII archives on 2 March 2020; 'The Church is not afraid of history; rather, she loves it'
Checked October 2026: no announced opening date for John XXIII's (1958-63) pontificate files found; Vatican News Aug 2025 still gives October 1958 as the limit
On 15 February 2003, at John Paul II's direction, the Holy See opened its archives on relations with Germany for 1922-1939, including Pacelli's nunciature files from Munich and Berlin.

vt14_pius_files.topic: The Pius XII files opened 2 March 2020: findings and debate

claims.text: Opening 2 March 2020: Vatican Apostolic Archive and other Holy See archives; about 120 series, roughly 20,000 archival units, much digital; about 120 researchers at a time by reservation; only a pope can authorise access to predecessors' papers
Archives opening included the Secretariat of State's Section for Relations with States historical archive, CDF archive, Propaganda Fide, Congregation for the Eastern Churches
Francis 4 March 2019 spoke of 'moments of serious difficulties, of tormented decisions' and 'human and Christian prudence'

Hubert Wolf's Münster team (2020): Sept 1942 US inquiry with Jewish Agency report on killings in Warsaw and Lviv; a note confirms Pius read it; Vatican had Sheptytsky's letter (200,000 Jews killed in Ukraine) and an Italian businessman's report via Montini; Dell'Acqua memo doubted the report saying Jews tended to exaggerate; Vatican told the US it could not confirm; Wolf says the 11-volume ADSS omitted the memo

Kertzer, The Pope at War (Random House, June 2022): Pius focused on protecting the institutional Church, believed Hitler might win; used 7,000+ pages; memos reveal antisemitism among aides; 1939 back-channel via Prince Philipp von Hessen (met Pius 11 May 1939); Vatican intervened in October 1943 only for baptised or mixed-marriage Jews
Evans: Pius's main concern was 'to preserve the interests of the Church as an institution'; Cucchiara: forceful, well documented, but thin on rescue historiography and overstated novelty

Napolitano (L'Osservatore Romano, 21 June 2022): secret talks were known from ADSS vol.1 (1965); Hitler sought the deal; Pius set five conditions; Maglione warned Weizsäcker 16 Oct 1943; 'worn-out view' that Pius cared only for baptised Jews

Letter 14 December 1942 from Jesuit Lothar König to Robert Leiber reporting up to 6,000 Poles and Jews killed daily at Bełżec ('blast furnace'), from Rava Ruska; found by archivist Giovanni Coco; published in Corriere della Sera Sept 2023; cannot be certain Pius saw it; registered in the archive 2019; ten days before the Christmas 1942 message which said people 'marked down for death or gradual extinction' without naming Nazis or Jews

'Ebrei' series published online June 2022 at Francis's request (Gallagher): 170 volumes, nearly 40,000 files, more than 2,700 cases of requests for help by baptised and non-baptised Jews; for most the outcome not recorded; fully online Feb 2023 with an inventory of more than 2,500 requesters

Johan Ickx, Pius XII and the Jews (2021), head of the Section for Relations with States historical archive, presents the series as 'The list of Pius XII' (about 2,800 cases) and argues the Vatican aimed at 'saving every single human being'
